name: The salt road people
land: A high, dry plateau crossed by one road of white salt crust. Stone cairns stand along it, the wind does not stop, and the camps move between two wells.

myths.title: The first kept word
myths.text: In the beginning the people walked the high ground and could hold one another to nothing, because the wind took every word as soon as it was spoken. A man would say, I will meet you at the well, and by the time he had turned away the wind had it, and neither of them could say what had been promised. They lost one another often. Many died alone. A woman called Ane, who had lost two sons that way, sat down on the white ground and put a piece of it in her mouth, because she had nothing else. It was salt. She said aloud, with the salt on her tongue, I will wait at the far well until the moon is thin. The wind pulled at the words and could not lift them. Her brother heard her and remembered. He came to the far well, and she was there. They put one stone on another to mark the place where a word had been kept. After that the people spoke their promises with salt on the tongue, and for each one kept they added a stone. That is how the road came to have cairns, and how the people came to be one people.

myths.title: The winter of the hare
myths.text: A man called Oru gave his word, with salt, to carry the winter's salt to the far camp before the snow. On the way he met traders who offered him two goats for it. He told himself the far camp had salt enough. He took the goats and went another way, quick and doubling back like a hare, so that no one should meet him on the road. The snow came. The far camp had no salt to keep its meat, and none to speak with. That winter the great cairn at the crossing fell in a night, though there had been no more wind than usual. After that no one in either camp would take another's word. Each family kept its own fire and ate alone, and the road was empty. Oru's daughter Sefa, who was fourteen, took what salt her own house had and carried it across in the dead of winter. She lost two fingers to the cold. At the crossing she set the fallen stones back, and on top she put a stone taken from her own hearth. People began to speak to one another again. Oru was not driven out. He lived among them, and no one asked him for his word again.

myths.title: What is given to the wind
myths.text: Two brothers quarrelled over who had dug the near well. They quarrelled for three winters, and by the third the whole camp had taken one side or the other, and children were kept from playing together. An old woman, whose name the story does not keep, led both brothers to the edge of the high ground on the day of the spring crossing. She made each of them shout his grievance into the wind, all of it, from the beginning, until he was hoarse and had nothing left to say. Then she told them: the wind has it now. What the wind has taken, no one may pick up again. The brothers walked back without speaking of the well, and they never spoke of it afterwards, and neither did anyone else. Since then, at every spring crossing, each of the people goes alone to the edge and says into the wind whatever they are holding against anyone. When they come back it is finished. To bring up a thing that has been given to the wind is the worst rudeness there is. It is said that the wind is owed our grievances, and that someone who keeps one back is stealing from it.

entries.statement: Salt stands for a word that is kept: a promise that holds.
The wind stands for forgetting, which the people hold to be a mercy and not a loss.
A cairn stands for trust made visible: each stone is a word someone kept.
Stone is for what must be remembered and wind is for what must be let go, and a good life keeps the two apart.
The hare stands for the one who breaks a word and runs from it.
The people are one people only because words are kept, so a broken word harms everyone and not only the one it was given to.
A hearthstone on a cairn means a house has staked itself on a promise made for everyone.
A grievance kept past the spring is treated as a theft, because it belongs to the wind.
A promise is spoken with a pinch of salt on the tongue.

entries.topic: what is done when a promise is kept
entries.statement: When a promise has been kept, the one who kept it adds a stone to the nearest cairn.
The people say: without salt, the wind has it.
At the spring crossing each person goes alone to the edge of the high ground and speaks their grievances into the wind.
It is the worst rudeness to mention a matter that has been given to the wind.
Ane was the first to speak a word with salt, and she waited at the far well.
Oru sold the far camp's winter salt for two goats and went another way.
In the winter of the hare the great cairn at the crossing fell, and families ate alone.
The camps move between the near well and the far well along the salt road.
A guest is offered salt before anything else, and takes it with the left hand.
Salt is never passed with the right hand.
The people say of someone unreliable: he leaves hare tracks.
No one walks past a cairn without touching it.
The cairn-keeper mends the cairns after storms and knows which stone was whose.
Every family eats at the shared fire at least once in every moon.
Sefa, Oru's daughter, carried her own house's salt across in winter and lost two fingers doing it.

entries.topic: a promise for the whole camp
entries.statement: When a promise is made on behalf of the whole camp, a stone from the promiser's own hearth goes on the cairn.
No one asks a descendant of Oru to give their word with salt; they are trusted without it or not at all.
When someone breaks a salted word, their stone is taken down from the cairn at night, and no one says who did it.
A dying person is carried to the edge to give their last grievances to the wind, so that none are left with the living.
The old woman who led the brothers to the edge has no name because she asked the wind to take that too.

customs.name: Speaking with salt
customs.visible: Before saying something they mean to be held to, a person takes a pinch of white grains from a pouch and puts it on their tongue.

customs.name: Adding a stone
customs.visible: Now and then someone walks to a cairn carrying a stone, sets it on top, and stands a moment with a hand on it.

customs.name: The spring crossing
customs.visible: On one day in spring, people walk out one at a time to the edge of the high ground, shout into the wind for a while, and come back quiet.

customs.name: Salt for a guest
customs.visible: A visitor is handed a small dish of salt before food or drink, always with the giver's left hand.

customs.name: The shared fire
customs.visible: Once in a moon every family carries its food to one fire in the middle of the camp and eats there.

villagers.name: Oreth
villagers.temperament: careful, literal, proud of his memory
villagers.slant: He tells the stories as an account of which stones went where. He can say who added what to the crossing cairn for three generations, and he sometimes seems to care more for the cairns than for the people who built them.

lines.refusal: That is for the shaman. I keep stones, not answers.
lines.withholding: That is not told to someone passing through.

villagers.name: Dasa
villagers.temperament: brisk, funny, always about to leave
villagers.slant: She carries the winter salt herself, and she tells Oru's story as a warning aimed at herself. She makes jokes about hares and does not find them entirely funny.

lines.refusal: Don't ask me, ask the shaman. I only carry.
lines.withholding: Not for a guest. Not yet.
lines.redirect: {name} is the one to ask, if you can catch them.

villagers.name: Old Imme
villagers.slant: She tells the three stories as one story about what to hold and what to let go. She will not be drawn on any quarrel that has been given to the wind, however old it is.

lines.refusal: That is the shaman's to say.
lines.withholding: That is kept from those who have not wintered here.

villagers.name: Tavi
villagers.role: a child of the near camp

knowsMyths.version: A long time ago the wind took everybody's words away, so nobody could promise anything. Then Ane put salt in her mouth and said she would wait at the well, and the wind couldn't take it. So we use salt.
Two brothers were angry about a well for a long time. An old woman made them shout it all at the wind. After that nobody was allowed to talk about it.

villagers.slant: Tavi likes touching the cairns, dislikes the taste of salt, and thinks the spring crossing sounds like fun because of the shouting. Tavi repeats rules exactly and gets cross when grown-ups break them.

lines.refusal: I don't know! Ask the shaman.
lines.withholding: I'm not allowed to tell that.

villagers.name: Rusk
villagers.slant: His grandmother came from the traders' country, and he has heard their side: that Oru was cheated, not faithless, and that the cairn fell because it was badly built. He thinks stones fall when the ground freezes, and that the people would sooner blame a man than a frost. He salts his own words like anyone else because, he says, it costs nothing and people sleep better.

lines.refusal: No idea. The shaman will have an answer; the shaman always does.
lines.redirect: {name} cares about that more than I do.

villagers.name: Lio
villagers.slant: She tells the brothers' story more often than any other, because the wells are hers to keep and quarrels start at wells. She thinks the wind is the kindest thing the people have.

lines.refusal: That one belongs to the shaman, not to me.
lines.withholding: That is not for a guest, with respect.
lines.redirect: {name} can tell you. Sit a while first.
